section.title: Score-level descriptors by criterion
section.paragraph: The rubric table explicitly describes levels 0, 1, 3, and 5. The source's general scoring rule defines levels 2 and 4 between those anchors (see scoring rules).

list.item: 5: (a) Supports the problem's existence with relevant evidence, such as published data, documented observations, or stakeholder input; (b) explains how the problem is currently handled and the specific shortcoming of that approach; (c) characterizes severity or frequency using a relevant measure, stating the source or assumptions.

3: (a) Identifies a specific user or stakeholder; (b) describes the situation where the problem occurs and its consequence; (c) defines the scope clearly enough to distinguish what the project addresses from what it does not.
1: Identifies a general problem and a broad group affected by it.
0: No identifiable problem is presented, or the submission describes a technology without explaining the problem it addresses.

5: (a) Compares at least two relevant alternatives, including the closest available approach; (b) explains why the contribution changes functionality, performance, or use in a meaningful way; (c) supports the claimed advantage through reasoned technical comparison, calculation, relevant evidence, or test, while identifying a trade-off or limitation.

3: (a) Identifies at least one relevant existing alternative; (b) specifically explains how the proposed solution differs; (c) explains how the difference could improve an outcome such as accuracy, cost, speed, reliability, accessibility, or usability.
1: Identifies a proposed difference, such as a new application, feature, method, integration, or adaptation.
0: No distinct contribution is identifiable; the submission repeats an existing approach without explaining a meaningful change or adaptation.

section.title: C3. Solution design and expected effectiveness (20%)

list.item: 5: (a) Specifies a measurable success criterion and explains why the proposed target would meaningfully address the problem; (b) identifies relevant failure situations or limitations and explains the intended response, safeguard, or boundary of use.

3: (a) Explains the main inputs, processing or operating steps, and outputs; (b) identifies the role of the space technology or data, and AI/ML where required by the chosen domain; (c) explains how the intended user would use the output to address the problem.
1: Describes the proposed solution and its intended output or benefit.
0: No understandable solution is presented, or there is no explained connection between the proposed solution and the problem.

5: (a) Supports the central technical assumption with relevant literature, calculations, analysis, or tests; (b) provides an approximate implementation timeline and major cost/resource estimates, with assumptions stated; (c) identifies the two most consequential implementation risks, or explains why fewer apply, and proposes a mitigation or fallback for each.

3: (a) Identifies the specific technologies, datasets, hardware, or services needed and explains their suitability; (b) identifies essential assumptions and dependencies, including how required resources could be accessed; (c) describes a plausible sequence of work and the main resources needed to reach an initial pilot or test.
1: Identifies a plausible technical approach and some resources it would require.
0: Provides no assessable implementation approach, or the central mechanism is technically untenable and the team provides no credible alternative.

5: (a) Demonstrates the main functions working together through a representative end-to-end use case; (b) compares results against a relevant baseline or predefined acceptance threshold; (c) tests at least one important failure condition or operating limitation and reports what the evidence shows about reliability or applicability.

3: (a) Implements or analytically demonstrates at least one core function through code, hardware, simulation, or worked data analysis; (b) provides inspectable evidence of operation, including inputs, outputs, and test conditions; (c) evaluates that function against at least one stated requirement relevant to the proposed solution.
1: Presents a developed concept through a coherent architecture, technical design, workflow, mock-up, or worked example. A functioning core component has not yet been demonstrated.
0: Presents an idea or intended benefits without an inspectable design, worked example, or implementation artifact.

section.title: C6. Saudi-market relevance and potential impact (15%)

list.item: 5: (a) Supports the proposed local application with relevant Saudi evidence or documented stakeholder input; (b) estimates at least one measurable benefit, with transparent assumptions and a basis for the estimate; (c) explains a plausible adoption pathway, including who would operate or adopt the solution and how it would fit their workflow.

3: (a) Defines a specific Saudi user and application context; (b) identifies a local condition affecting design or deployment, such as geography, infrastructure, operating practices, or available resources; (c) explains a causal link between using the solution and a relevant benefit for that user.
1: Names a Saudi sector, user group, organization type, or issue that could benefit.
0: Provides no identifiable Saudi beneficiary or application context.

section.title: C7. Presentation and responses to questions (10%)

list.item: 5: (a) Covers essential content within the allotted presentation time; (b) clearly distinguishes what is proposed, implemented, and tested, and separates estimates from measured results; (c) supports answers with relevant reasoning or evidence and identifies uncertainties rather than making unsupported claims.

3: (a) Presents the problem, approach, and expected benefit in a logical sequence; (b) uses readable materials and explains essential terminology, diagrams, and figures; (c) answers questions directly enough for judges to understand the team's reasoning.
1: Communicates an identifiable problem and proposed solution.
0: No assessable presentation is provided, or the audience cannot identify the problem and proposed solution.
Score 0: The criterion is absent or meets its specific zero-score description.
Score 1: The submission meets the basic description for the criterion.
Score 2: The submission meets score-1 requirements and some, but not all, score-3 requirements.
Score 3: The submission meets all listed score-3 requirements.
Score 4: The submission meets score-3 requirements and some, but not all, additional score-5 requirements.
Score 5: The submission meets all score-3 requirements and all additional score-5 requirements.
If a submission's problem does not fit the chosen domain, assign 0 for Problem definition and specificity.
Failure to use AI or Machine Learning in Satellite Protection or Earth Observation and AI results in 0 for Solution design and expected effectiveness.
A score of 0 in Problem definition and specificity, Originality and Differentiation, and/or Solution design and expected effectiveness limits every other criterion to a maximum score of 2.
Tie-breakers: Saudi-market relevance and potential impact, then Technical and implementation feasibility.
Technical correctness should inform the relevant technical criterion. The Presentation criterion assesses communication and should not depend on accent, expensive graphics, or theatrical delivery.
Intent: Assess how clearly the team establishes the problem and the need to address it.
Questions: Does the team identify the affected user, the context in which the problem occurs, and evidence that it matters?
Intent: Assess the team's contribution relative to existing approaches.

Questions: What improves on existing approaches? Is the contribution meaningful within the Saudi market? An inventive application of existing technology can score highly when its advantage is explained.

section.title: C3. Solution design and expected effectiveness

list.item: Intent: Assess whether the design explains a convincing route from the identified problem to a useful outcome. A concept can receive full marks.
Questions: Does the team explain how the solution works and why it addresses the problem? Are inputs, method, outputs, and the role of the used technology clear?
Intent: Assess whether there is a credible route to implementing the proposed solution. A concept can receive full marks.

Questions: Are the scientific assumptions credible? Are required data, technology, skills, and resources obtainable? Does the team recognize major limitations, estimate key costs, and propose a realistic validation plan?
Intent: Give explicit additional credit for more completed solutions; assess what the team can substantiate at the submission deadline.

Questions: Which core functions have been demonstrated? What remains conceptual or unimplemented? How complete is the demonstrated workflow? Does it cover an isolated component or a representative end-to-end use case?

section.title: C6. Saudi-market relevance and potential impact

list.item: Intent: Assess fit with a specific Saudi context and the value the solution could create there. A concept can receive full marks.
Questions: Is there a specific Saudi user, organization, or sector that could benefit? Does the concept account for local operating conditions? Are the expected benefits reasonably supported?

section.title: C7. Presentation and responses to questions

list.item: Intent: Assess communication; it should not depend on accent, expensive graphics, or theatrical delivery.
Questions: Is the explanation clear, organized, and within the time limit? Do visuals aid understanding? Does the team answer questions directly and acknowledge uncertainty?
